2012.insight: Monetary Policy dominated Chilean economic discourse in 2012, reflecting the Banco Central's active management of a commodity-driven expansion — copper revenues were near historic highs and inflation targeting required continuous calibration. The strong co-presence of International Trade (15.5%) and Macroeconomic Outlook (14.9%) reveals a media environment intensely attentive to Chile's external exposure, while persistently negative sentiment (−0.24) suggests that even during a growth cycle, framing remained cautious — a pattern consistent with the hedging behaviour of export-oriented business elites who discount boom narratives and price in eventual reversals.

2013.insight: Monetary Policy retained its primacy in 2013 (20.3%), amplified by an electoral cycle that pushed Government & Politics to a secondary peak as Bachelet's reform programme became the central frame for business media — markets were pricing in fiscal expansion before the votes were counted. The slight deepening of negative sentiment (−0.26) relative to 2012 points to anticipatory anxiety: the financial press was already discounting the tax and educational reforms promised by the incoming centre-left coalition, a narrative that would directly condition private investment expectations throughout 2014.

2014.insight: The shift to Government & Politics as the dominant topic in 2014 (20.9%) precisely marks the moment when structural reform — not the business cycle — became the primary lens through which Chilean economic media interpreted reality. The Bachelet II government's simultaneous pursuit of tax, education, and labour reform compressed attention onto executive-branch decisions, crowding out trade and investment coverage. Sentiment improved slightly (−0.22) but remained firmly negative, consistent with a period in which uncertainty about the scope of reform translated into deferred corporate investment — a narrative-driven coordination failure that Chilean GDP data would later reflect.

2015.insight: The copper crash of September 2015 did not produce a discrete media spike but instead diffused into a broadly distributed discourse structure — with Monetary Policy, Government & Politics, Legal & Judiciary, and Macroeconomic Outlook all clustering near 10–15% — signalling that no single narrative frame was sufficient to contain the shock. This fragmentation of attention is itself informative: it reflects genuine uncertainty about the transmission channel, whether the copper correction would hit fiscal accounts, employment, exchange rates, or investment flows. Sentiment held at −0.23, suggesting that the financial press had already incorporated a downside scenario into its baseline, dampening the marginal pessimism the commodity crash might otherwise have generated.

2016.insight: Monetary Policy re-emerged as the dominant frame in 2016 (17.9%), as the Banco Central navigated the post-copper-crash slowdown through a sequence of rate adjustments that received sustained media attention. The relatively elevated weight of Corporate Finance (10%) alongside Macroeconomic Outlook (10.5%) points to a year in which market participants were actively seeking leading indicators of recovery — making financial media a coordination mechanism for investment timing decisions. The modest sentiment improvement (−0.22) suggests a gradual recalibration of expectations, but the negative baseline persisted, consistent with an economy still absorbing the fiscal consequences of lower commodity revenues.

2017.insight: The most notable feature of 2017 is the sharp improvement in sentiment (−0.17, the least negative in the entire sample) that preceded and accompanied the Piñera II election — a textbook case of narrative-driven expectation formation, where business media shifted tone in advance of the electoral outcome rather than in response to it. Monetary Policy and Government & Politics led the discourse in roughly equal measure, while a notable recovery in Corporate Finance (10.6%) and Investment & Energy (10.1%) suggests that the financial press was already pricing in a more investment-friendly policy environment. This anticipatory positive reframing likely contributed to the actual recovery in private investment that materialised in 2018.

2018.insight: Government & Politics returned to dominance in 2018 (13.8%) as the Piñera administration's deregulation and investment-incentive agenda became the primary editorial frame — reflecting business media's alignment with the new government's economic programme. The balanced distribution across International Trade (9.6%), Macroeconomic Outlook (12.7%), and Investment & Energy (8.6%) indicates that the discourse was genuinely pluralistic rather than concentrated, consistent with a year of broad-based economic optimism. Yet sentiment (−0.19) remained materially negative, suggesting that structural pessimism — embedded in editorial convention and Chilean financial journalism's characteristic risk-consciousness — persisted even as macro conditions improved.

2019.insight: The Estallido Social of October 2019 is clearly legible in the year's discourse structure: Government & Politics (14.7%) and Labor & Society (14.0%) achieved near-parity for the first time in the sample, reflecting the social uprising's dual nature as both a political crisis and a deep-seated distributional complaint. The simultaneous elevation of Pension & Tax Reform (9.7%) signals that the financial press rapidly reframed the unrest through the lens of structural reform demands rather than treating it as episodic disorder. Sentiment (−0.19) remained negative but — strikingly — did not deteriorate sharply relative to prior years, suggesting that Chilean business media had partially normalised political uncertainty as a permanent feature of the landscape rather than an acute shock.

2020.insight: Pension & Tax Reform surged to dominance in 2020 (14.6%) — a result not of a budget cycle but of the extraordinary AFP early-withdrawal legislation, which injected pension savings directly into household liquidity during the COVID-19 lockdown. The near-simultaneous elevation of Macroeconomic Outlook (13.3%) and Monetary Policy (13.0%) reflects a media environment scrambling to frame an economic shock with no historical precedent in Chile. The sharp deterioration of sentiment (−0.25, matching the 2012 low) captures the collective anxiety of an economy facing simultaneous supply, demand, and public-health shocks — a framing that likely deepened precautionary saving and suppressed consumption beyond what the underlying conditions alone would have produced.

2021.insight: Pension & Tax Reform retained its dominant position in 2021 (14.2%), as the constituent assembly election and the Boric presidential campaign both centred distributional questions — pension privatisation, tax progressivity, and public health financing — as the core political-economic fault lines. The high Labor & Society share (12.2%) reflects the pandemic's enduring recomposition of Chile's labour market, while Monetary Policy (12.7%) captured the Banco Central's pivot toward tightening as inflation re-emerged globally. The partial sentiment recovery (−0.19) likely reflects a post-AFP-withdrawal liquidity effect that temporarily boosted consumption and corporate earnings coverage, even as medium-term institutional uncertainty remained unresolved.

2022.insight: The constitutional referendum's rejection in September 2022 coincides with Monetary Policy returning to dominance (16.0%) as the Banco Central executed one of the most aggressive tightening cycles in Chilean history to contain inflation running above 13% — the sharpest price surge since the 1990s. Macroeconomic Outlook (13.5%) remained elevated, reflecting sustained uncertainty about fiscal consolidation after three years of pandemic-era spending and AFP withdrawals. The deterioration of sentiment back to −0.25 captures the convergence of multiple headwinds — inflation, monetary tightening, a contracting economy, and the political exhaustion of a failed constitutional process — into a coherent negative narrative that would condition business investment decisions well into 2023.

2023.insight: Monetary Policy sustained its dominance in 2023 (16.5%) as the Banco Central began its rate-cutting cycle from a peak of 11.25%, generating sustained media attention on the timing and pace of monetary normalisation. The persistent elevation of Macroeconomic Outlook (12.8%) alongside Pension & Tax Reform (10.0%) reflects a year in which three major reform processes — pension, tax, and the second constitutional draft — were simultaneously active, maintaining an unusually high policy uncertainty premium in the financial press. Sentiment (−0.25) showed no improvement from 2022, confirming that the second constitutional rejection in December did not resolve the underlying institutional uncertainty but merely deferred it — a narrative outcome with measurable consequences for the investment climate.

2024.insight: The 2024 discourse structure reveals a gradual normalisation after four years of acute political-economic volatility: Monetary Policy (14.5%) and Macroeconomic Outlook (12.5%) co-dominated a more balanced distribution, with no topic exceeding 15% for the first time since 2018. The modest sentiment improvement (−0.23) aligns with the Banco Central's successful disinflation, falling rates, and the end of the constitutional process — but the persistent negativity of the baseline confirms that Chilean financial journalism had structurally recalibrated toward a more cautious register following the 2019–2023 shock sequence, a framing bias that may itself dampen the recovery in business confidence that orthodox macroeconomic models would predict from these underlying conditions.
